name: Cetilistat
lead: Cetilistat (ATL-962) is a pancreatic lipase inhibitor developed as an anti-obesity drug. Like orlistat, it blocks intestinal enzymes that break down dietary fat, so some ingested fat is excreted rather than absorbed.[1][2]
It completed Phase 1 and 2 trials in Western countries and was developed in Japan with Takeda, which reportedly obtained approval to market it there. Takeda ended its license with Norgine in 2018.[1]

Phase 2 trials reported weight loss in obese patients and, in people with type 2 diabetes, weight and HbA1c reductions with tolerability described as comparable to or better than orlistat.[3][4] It does not have broad international availability.
infobox: Marketed in Japan per Wikipedia; not broadly approved elsewhere

paras: A phase II, multicentre, randomized, placebo-controlled 12-week study of 442 obese patients (371 randomized after a hypocaloric diet run-in) examined cetilistat's efficacy, safety and tolerability.[3] A 12-week trial in obese patients with type 2 diabetes on metformin compared cetilistat at three doses with orlistat and placebo; the primary endpoint was body weight change, and secondary endpoints included other obesity measures.[4] Wikipedia summarises the 2007 study as showing weight loss similar to orlistat, and the 2010 trial as showing significant weight reduction, HbA1c reduction and better tolerability than orlistat.[1]

Registered phase 1 and 2 trials (NCT00148382, NCT00156897) examined fat excretion and efficacy in obese diabetics.[5][6] Reviews of obesity drugs in development have described cetilistat among the lipase inhibitors beyond orlistat.[7][8] A study in rats reported reduced body weight gain and improved lipid profiles.[9]

Reported effects mirror orlistat: oily or loose stools, fecal incontinence, frequent bowel movements and flatulence. Because fat-soluble vitamin absorption may also be reduced, supplementation may be needed to prevent deficiencies.[1]
Cetilistat inhibits gastrointestinal lipases, preventing hydrolysis of dietary triglycerides, so unabsorbed fat is excreted.[1][3]
Alizyme developed the drug and went into administration; Norgine BV then acquired the global rights. By 2009 it was in Phase 3 trials in Japan with Takeda.[1]
A 2020 screening study of approved drugs identified cetilistat as having anti-SARS-CoV-2 activity in vitro.[10] This is unrelated to its weight-loss use.

timeline.event: Phase 3 trials under way in Japan with Takeda.[1]
Phase 2 trial in obese diabetics versus orlistat published.[4]
Takeda ends license agreement with Norgine.[1]

card.summary: An orlistat-style fat-blocking pill with phase 2 data and limited availability outside Japan.
card.note: Fat-blocker with orlistat-like GI side effects; not broadly approved.

quick.overview:
Cetilistat is a drug that blocks fat-digesting enzymes so some dietary fat passes out of the body. Phase 2 trials reported weight loss, with side effects similar to orlistat but possibly better tolerated.

It was developed by Alizyme, Takeda and Norgine and is reportedly approved in Japan.
quick.mechanism: It inhibits pancreatic and gastrointestinal lipases, so triglycerides are not broken down and absorbed.
quick.risks: Side effects are digestive (oily stools, urgency, flatulence), and fat-soluble vitamin absorption may be reduced. It is not widely available.
